title: Process goals and the score
summary: Why goals about what you do tend to help more than goals about winning, and how to set goals for your first competition.

body.html: There are three kinds of goals. A process goal is about how you shoot: “the full routine on each target”. A personal standard is your own level: “22 of 25 on this layout”. An outcome goal is about the result: “win” or “top three”.

In a review of 27 studies, process goals helped results the most, personal standards helped some, and outcome goals hardly at all. Some of these findings rest on only a few studies, so the reliable part is the order: process first, then your personal standard, then the outcome. The studies are not from clay shooting, so most likely this works the same way in Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting.
An outcome also depends on others: you can shoot very well and still lose. A process goal stays in your hands on each target.

html: Choose two or three process goals, for example “full routine on each target”, “reset after each miss”, “eyes on the target”.
Add one realistic personal standard based on your training scores.
Leave outcome goals at home: no “I must finish in the top ten”.
Write the goals down the night before and read them in the morning.
After the event, check each goal: kept or not? Note one thing to keep and one to train.

body.html: Do not count your score while you shoot a stand. Look at it once the stand is over, then go back to your process goals.
Sporting™ has a rule for that moment: when you leave the stand, check that your score on the card is right (Chapter 16 · Recording results and checking your score).

For juniors, process goals take pressure off, because they reward what the child controls. In studies, young athletes were less anxious when their coaches cared more about learning than about winning: see Juniors and parents: support without pressure.
Keep your goals and the after-event check in your training diary: over a season you will see which goals helped.

notes.html: Before a competition, agree two or three process goals with the shooter, and ask about them afterwards before you ask about the score.

key_points.html: Process goals about how you shoot tend to help more than goals about winning.
Set 2–3 process goals and one realistic personal standard.
Check the score on the card, not during the stand.
After the event, review each goal: kept or not.

did_you_know.html: Some shooters treat a round of 25 targets as 25 small competitions of one target each. It is another way of saying “one target at a time”.

quiz.explain: A process goal is about how you shoot, which stays in your hands on each target.

quiz.q: Which kind of goal helped results the most in research?
quiz.explain: Process goals helped the most, personal standards somewhat, outcome goals hardly at all.

quiz.q: What kind of goal is “22 of 25 on this layout”?
quiz.explain: It is your own standard: it sits between a process goal and an outcome goal.
